newsitem.title: UK: British brewers agree changes to "alcopop" images.
newsitem.headline: British brewers agree changes to "alcopop" images.

text.p: British brewers have agreed to change marketing of alcoholic fruit-flavoured drinks, so-called "alcopops" after complaints that they targeted drinkers under the legal limit of 18 were upheld by an industry body.
Bass will remove its smiling fruit image from its "Hoopers Hooch" brand while Whitbread will change the name of its Lemon Jag and Vanilla Heist alcopops.
Neither Bass nor Whitbread have decided on replacements yet.

The moves came in response to a report on complaints about marketing of alcopops which was published on Wednesday by the Portman Group, a body funded by seven leading brewers and distillers to promote sensible drinking.
The industry body also persuaded Spilt Drinks to remove a cartoon character from its Jammin' brand.

"Today's report shows that self-regulation is working. Drinks companies have show their commitment to the code comes before short-term brand considerations," Portman Group director Jean Coussins said in a statement.
Neither Bass nor Whitbread will remove current stocks from sale but said the changes would be made once existing packaging was exhausted.
Bass maintained that there was no evidence to suggest that the images used were attracting under-age drinkers but said it accepted the opinion of the Portman Group.
Carlsberg-Tetley, whose alcopops include Lemonhead and Orangehead, escaped criticism from the group.
But the company described as "premature" a report in the Financial Times that it had decided not to sell its new Thickhead line in shops and off-licences.
"No final decision on any aspect of Thickhead marketing has yet been made," a spokesman said.
The Portman Group said Carlsberg-Tetley had agreed to re-label Thickhead last month and the company said the label was within Portman Group guidelines.
The Portman Group, of which Bass and Whitbread are both founder members, said one in five complaints considered had been upheld.
Alcopops have been sharply criticised by alcohol concern groups who say they target under-age drinkers. Alcohol in Britain can be sold only to those over the age of 18.
"If parents, doctors, teachers or anyone else is concerned about a drinks product or the way it is sold, the code enables them to bring a complaint to our attention," Coussins said in the statement.
Sixteen complaints that drinks targeted under-age drinking were thrown out, the Portman Group said.
